final_text: "However, concealing the madwoman's presence from you was something like covering a child with a cloak and laying it near a poison tree: that demon's proximity is toxic, and always was. But I will shut up Thornfield Hall. I will nail up the front door and board the lower windows. I will pay Mrs. Poole two hundred a year to live here with my wife, as you call that fearful hag. Grace will do much for money, and she shall have her son—the keeper at Grimsby Retreat—to bear her company and help her during the fits, when my wife is driven by her demons to burn people in their beds at night, to stab them, to bite the flesh from their bones, and so on—"

As for the new existence, it's exactly right: you shall still be my wife. I am not married. You shall be Mrs. Rochester—both in reality and in name. I shall be faithful only to you for as long as we both live. You shall go to a place I have in the south of France: a whitewashed villa on the shores of the Mediterranean. There you shall live a happy, protected, and perfectly innocent life. Never fear that I wish to lure you into sin—to make you my mistress. Why did you shake your head? final_text: "Well, Jane, being so, he was determined to keep the estate intact. He could not bear the thought of dividing his property and leaving me a fair share: everything, he resolved, should go to my brother Rowland. Yet he could not stand the idea of a son of his being a poor man. I had to be provided for through a wealthy marriage. He found me a match early on. Mr. Mason, a West Indian planter and merchant, was an old acquaintance of his. My father confirmed that his wealth was real and vast; he made inquiries. Mr. Mason, he discovered, had a son and a daughter; and he learned that Mason could and would give the daughter a fortune of thirty thousand pounds. That was enough. When I left university, I was sent to Jamaica to marry a bride who had already been chosen for me. My father said nothing about her money, but he told me Miss Mason was the beauty of Spanish Town—and that was no lie. I found her a striking woman, in the style of Blanche Ingram: tall, dark, and majestic. Her family wanted to secure me because I came from good stock; and so did she. They showed her to me at parties, magnificently dressed. I rarely saw her alone and had very little private conversation with her. She flattered me and lavishly displayed her charms and accomplishments for my pleasure. Every man in her circle seemed to admire her and envy me. I was dazzled, excited. My senses were aroused; and being ignorant, inexperienced, and naive, I thought I loved her. There is no folly so absurd that the stupid rivalries of society, the lust, the recklessness, the blindness of youth, will not drive a man to commit it. Her relatives encouraged me; rivals goaded me; she seduced me: a marriage was accomplished almost before I knew what had happened. Oh, I have no respect for myself when I think of that act!—an agony of inward shame overwhelms me. I never loved her, I never respected her, I did not even know her. I was not sure of a single virtue in her nature. I had seen neither modesty, nor kindness, nor honesty, nor refinement in her mind or manners—and I married her: gross, groveling, blind fool that I was! With less sin I might have—but let me remember who I am speaking to."

final_text: "Pity, Jane, from some people is a poisonous and insulting kind of offering—the sort you are justified in hurling back in the faces of those who give it. But that is the pity born of callous, selfish hearts: a self-centered pain at hearing of suffering, mixed with ignorant contempt for those who have endured it. But that is not your pity, Jane. It is not the feeling that fills your whole face at this moment—that brims in your eyes—that heaves in your chest—that trembles through the hand you have placed in mine. Your pity, my darling, is the suffering mother of love: its anguish is the birth-pang of that divine passion. I accept it, Jane; let the daughter be born freely—my arms are ready to receive her."

final_text: "I can tell you whether I found anyone I liked, and whether I asked her to marry me. But what she said is yet to be recorded in the book of Fate. For ten long years I roamed, living first in one capital, then another: sometimes in St. Petersburg, more often in Paris, occasionally in Rome, Naples, and Florence. With plenty of money and the passport of an old family name, I could choose my own company. No circles were closed to me. I looked for my ideal of a woman among English ladies, French countesses, Italian signoras, and German noblewomen. I could not find her. Sometimes, for a fleeting moment, I thought I caught a glance, heard a voice, saw a figure that promised the fulfillment of my dream—but I was soon disappointed. You are not to think I demanded perfection, either of mind or body. I longed only for what suited me—for the opposite of the Creole. And I longed in vain. Among them all I found not one whom, had I been ever so free, I—warned as I was of the risks, the horrors, the revulsion of mismatched unions—would have asked to marry me. Disappointment made me reckless. I tried pleasure-seeking—never debauchery: that I hated, and still hate. That was the mark of my West Indian Messalina: a deep-rooted disgust at it and at her restrained me considerably, even in my pleasures. Any enjoyment that bordered on excess seemed to bring me closer to her and her vices, and I avoided it."

final_text: "On a frosty winter afternoon, I rode within sight of Thornfield Hall. Detested place! I expected no peace there—no pleasure. On a stile in Hay Lane I saw a quiet little figure sitting by itself. I passed it as carelessly as I did the pollarded willow across from it: I had no premonition of what it would be to me. No inner warning that the ruler of my life—my spirit for good or evil—waited there in humble form. I did not know it, even when, after Mesrour's accident, it came up and gravely offered to help me. Childish and slender creature! It seemed as if a linnet had hopped to my foot and offered to carry me on its tiny wing. I was surly; but the thing would not go away: it stood beside me with a strange persistence, and looked and spoke with a sort of authority. I was to be helped, and by that hand: and helped I was."

final_text: "I began to notice you again. There was something glad in your look and warm in your manner when you talked. I saw you had a social heart; it was the silent schoolroom—the tedium of your life—that made you melancholy. I allowed myself the pleasure of being kind to you; kindness stirred emotion quickly. Your face grew soft, your voice gentle. I liked hearing my name spoken by your lips in a grateful, happy tone. I used to enjoy a chance meeting with you, Jane, in those days. There was a curious hesitation in your manner: you glanced at me with a slight unease—a hovering doubt. You did not know what my mood might be—whether I would play the master and be stern, or the friend and be warm. I was now too fond of you to often pretend the first; and when I extended my hand warmly, such color and light and joy rose in your young, wistful face that I could barely keep myself from pulling you right then and there to my heart."

final_text: "You see now how things stand—do you not?" he continued. "After a youth and manhood spent half in unspeakable misery and half in dreary solitude, I have for the first time found what I can truly love—I have found you. You are my kindred spirit—my better self—my good angel. I am bound to you with a powerful attachment. I think you good, gifted, and lovely: a fervent, solemn passion has been conceived in my heart. It leans toward you, draws you to the center and wellspring of my life, wraps my existence around you, and, burning in a pure, powerful flame, fuses you and me into one."

final_text: "It was because I felt and knew this that I resolved to marry you. To tell me I already had a wife is meaningless: you know now that I had only a hideous demon. I was wrong to try to deceive you; but I feared a stubbornness in your character. I feared prejudices instilled in you early. I wanted to have you safe before risking any confessions. This was cowardly: I should have appealed to your nobility and generosity from the start, as I do now—opened to you plainly my life of agony—described my hunger and thirst for a higher and worthier existence—shown you not my resolution (that word is too weak), but my irresistible drive to love faithfully and well, where I am faithfully and well loved in return. Then I should have asked you to accept my pledge of faithfulness and give me yours. Jane—give it to me now."

final_text: This was true. And while he spoke, my very conscience and reason turned traitor against me and accused me of a crime in resisting him. final_text: Still, the answer was unyielding—"I care for myself. The more alone, the more friendless, the more without support I am, the more I will respect myself. I will keep the law given by God, sanctioned by man. I will hold to the principles I received when I was sane, not mad—as I am now. Laws and principles are not for the times when there is no temptation: they are for moments like this, when body and soul rise in mutiny against their strictness. Strict they are; unbroken they shall stay. If at my individual convenience I might break them, what would they be worth? They have worth—so I have always believed; and if I cannot believe it now, it is because I am insane—quite insane, with fire running in my veins and my heart beating faster than I can count its throbs. Opinions formed beforehand, decisions made long ago, are all I have to stand by at this hour: there I plant my foot."

final_text: I did. Mr. Rochester, reading my face, saw that I had. His fury was worked up to its highest pitch: he had to yield to it for a moment, whatever followed. He crossed the floor, seized my arm, and gripped my waist. He seemed to devour me with his blazing gaze. Physically, at that moment, I felt as powerless as stubble exposed to the draught and glow of a furnace; mentally, I still possessed my soul, and with it the certainty of ultimate safety. The soul, fortunately, has an interpreter—often an unconscious, but still a truthful interpreter—in the eye. My eye rose to his; and as I looked into his fierce face, I gave an involuntary sigh: his grip was painful, and my overtaxed strength was almost exhausted.

Whatever I do with its cage, I cannot get at it—the savage, beautiful creature! If I tear, if I rip apart the flimsy prison, my violence will only set the captive free. final_text: Drearily I made my way downstairs. I knew what I had to do, and I did it mechanically. I found the key to the side door in the kitchen. I also found a small bottle of oil and a feather. I oiled the key and the lock. I got some water; I got some bread: for I might have to walk far, and my strength, badly shaken of late, must not break down. I did all this without a sound. I opened the door, stepped through it, and closed it softly. Dim dawn glimmered in the yard. The great gates were shut and locked, but a wicket set into one of them was only latched. I slipped out through that, and shut it too behind me; and now I was clear of Thornfield.

final_text: I skirted fields, hedges, and lanes until after sunrise. I believe it was a lovely summer morning: I know my shoes, which I had put on when I left the house, were soon wet with dew. But I looked neither at the rising sun, nor the smiling sky, nor the waking countryside. A man taken out to walk through a fair landscape to the scaffold does not think of the flowers smiling along his road, but of the block and the edge of the axe, of the parting of bone and vein, of the grave gaping at the end of it—and I thought of bleak flight and homeless wandering, and oh, with what agony I thought of what I had left behind. I could not help it. I thought of him now—in his room—watching the sunrise, hoping I would soon come to tell him I would stay and be his. I longed to be his; I ached to go back: it was not too late; I could still spare him the bitter pain of loss. My flight, I was sure, was still undiscovered. I could return and be his comfort, his pride, his redeemer from misery, perhaps from ruin. Oh, that fear of his self-abandonment—far worse than my own abandonment—how it goaded me! It was a barbed arrowhead lodged in my chest; it tore at me when I tried to pull it out; it sickened me every time the memory drove it deeper. Birds began singing in the thicket and the copse: birds were faithful to their mates; birds were symbols of love. What was I? In the middle of my heartbreak and my frantic effort to hold to principle, I despised myself. I found no comfort in self-approval, not even in self-respect. I had injured—wounded—left my master. I was hateful in my own eyes. Still I could not turn back, could not retrace a single step. God must have been leading me on. As for my own will or conscience, grief in its fury had trampled one and silenced the other. I wept wildly as I walked along my solitary way, going faster and faster like someone delirious. A weakness that began inside me and spread to my limbs seized me, and I fell: I lay on the ground for some minutes, my face pressed to the wet grass. I had some fear—or hope—that I would die there. But I was soon up again, crawling forward on my hands and knees, and then rising once more to my feet, as eager and as determined as ever to reach the road.

final_text: When I got there, I was forced to sit and rest under the hedge; and while I sat, I heard wheels, and saw a coach coming on. I stood up and raised my hand; it stopped. I asked where it was going: the driver named a place a long way off, somewhere I was sure Mr. Rochester had no connections. I asked what he would charge to take me there; he said thirty shillings. I told him I had only twenty; well, he said, he would try to make it do. He further let me ride inside, since the coach was empty: I got in, the door was shut, and it rolled on its way.
